title: Krishna eats at Vidura's
hookLine: Krishna sets out to make peace himself, carrying Draupadi's words with him, and in Hastinapura he turns down a royal feast
carry: bhava: God tastes the love, not the feast
tomorrow: why make the case for peace if he'll refuse?

cards: Krishna decides to go to Hastinapura himself: one more try for peace, in person. Before he leaves, each of the brothers gives him a message, and several of them lean toward peace. Then Draupadi comes to him.
She takes her long dark hair in her hand, the hair Duhshasana dragged her by in the dice hall, and holds it up. When you speak of peace, she says, remember this.
If my husbands won't fight, my old father will, and my sons will. Krishna promises her she'll see justice, and sets off.

teach.b: Duryodhana has rest houses built along the road and lays out a great feast. This is diplomacy as hospitality: if Krishna eats at his table, he's half won. Krishna passes the rest houses by.
In the city he greets the old king, then goes to Kunti, the Pandavas' mother, who has been living in Vidura's house all these years. She weeps and asks after her sons, one by one.
Only then does Krishna go to Duryodhana's palace. He accepts his greeting, and declines the meal. Duryodhana is offended.
Why won't you eat with us? Krishna's answer is short and sharp. A person eats another's food either out of love, or out of need.
You feel no love for me, and I'm in no need. So he walks back to a much plainer house: the home of Vidura, the wise half-brother of the king, who spoke up for the Pandavas years ago in the dice hall.
That's where Krishna eats, and where he stays. This is the root of something every Hindu kitchen knows.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, OFFERED WITH LOVE
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, and I accept it. What God receives is the bhava, the feeling, not the size of the plate.
That's why families offer food at the home shrine before anyone eats, and share it afterward as prasad. Duryodhana's banquet was a deal. Vidura's plain supper was love.

how: Krishna's refusal of Duryodhana's feast and his meal at Vidura's house are retold in Hindu devotional storytelling, often alongside the Gita's verse on the leaf, flower, fruit and water offered with love; many families offer food at the home shrine before eating.

s: Krishna ate at Duryodhana's feast to keep the peace
he declined it, saying people eat another's food out of love or need.
Draupadi asked Krishna to remember her hair when he spoke of peace
she held up the hair she was dragged by in the dice hall.

he says a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, offered with love, is accepted.

games.q: you're Krishna, come to Hastinapura to talk peace. Duryodhana has laid out a grand feast in your honor. what do you do?
o: eat, and use the goodwill in tomorrow's talks.
decline: people share food out of love or need, and here there's neither.
eat a little and leave early.
games.why: Krishna declines, says exactly that, and goes to eat at Vidura's plain house instead.

practice: Before your next meal or snack, pause and offer it, the way many Hindu families do at the home shrine: hold it a moment and, if you pray, offer it silently to God with love before you eat.
If you don't pray, think of the hands it came through and be glad of them. Then eat slowly, as if it were prasad.

orig.note: effort, getting ready; in this book Krishna's own journey to Hastinapura is part of the effort for peace.
